To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the anthropometric measures of BMI, WC, WC:H, WC:Ht, conicity index, and %BF were all significant predictors of increased fasting glucose and TG, but none of the measures were significant predictors of increased total cholesterol in physically active women over the age of 50 years.

the anthropometric measures of body mass index, waist circumference, waist-hip ratio, and waist-height ratio, and the percentage of body fat were all able to discriminate increased blood glucose, and that only the waist-hip ratio was able to discriminate increased triglycerides.
BMI, WC, WHR, WHtR, and %BF can discriminate increased blood glucose, while only WHR can discriminate increased triglycerides in physically active women over the age of 50 years.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of anthropometric variables as predictors for the presence of metabolic disorders in women over 50 years of age.
the relationship between the anthropometric variables and the biochemical variables in women over the age of 50 years who practice physical activity.
the relationship between anthropometric measurements and biochemical alterations (cholesterol, triglycerides and glucose levels) in physically active women over the age of 50 years.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no clear evidence that anthropometry is an effective tool to identify metabolic risk factors in physically active postmenopausal women.
the anthropometric measurements were not good predictors of metabolic alterations in this sample of older women.
the anthropometric measures used in this research are able to discriminate biochemical alterations in physically active women aged over 50 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the anthropometric measures of body composition can discriminate some of the biochemical alterations in the elderly women.
anthropometric measures may be useful for the screening of metabolic alterations in older women.
the risk of altered biochemical parameters, glycemia and triglycerides, can be discriminated by some anthropometric variables in women over 50 years old who practice physical activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have identified a new mechanism by which a common genetic variant may contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes, and that this may be through the regulation of the expression of a key enzyme in glucose metabolism.

the use of anthropometric measures in the assessment of metabolic risk in women is not as straightforward as it may seem, and that a more holistic approach, taking into account the individual’s body composition and physical activity, may provide a more comprehensive picture of the metabolic status of the individual.
there are a number of anthropometric measures that can help identify women over the age of 50 with higher levels of blood glucose and triglycerides.
